units.title: Complexity & Data Structures
units.blurb: Pick the right structure and the algorithm often writes itself.

bites.title: Big-O Notation
bites.tldr: Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows, ignoring constants.
points: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n log n) good sorting, O(n²) nested loops, O(2ⁿ) explosive.
Drop constants and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²).
Talk about worst case unless asked otherwise; mention average case for hashing and quicksort.
Space complexity counts extra memory, including the recursion stack.
bites.formula: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)
bites.example: Two nested loops over n items do n × n = n² steps; one loop with a hash lookup inside is O(n).
bites.tip: Ask yourself: how many times does the innermost line run as n doubles?

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of binary search?
quiz.why: Each step halves the remaining range, so about log₂ n steps.

bites.say: Big-O Notation. Big-O describes how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows, ignoring constants. O of one constant, O of log n halving, O of n linear, O of n log n good sorting, O of n squared nested loops, O of 2 to the n explosive. Drop constants and smaller terms: 3n squared plus 5n plus 2 is O of n squared. Talk about worst case unless asked otherwise; mention average case for hashing and quicksort. Space complexity counts extra memory, including the recursion stack. In order from fastest to slowest: constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic, exponential and factorial. Example: Two nested loops over n items do n times n equals n squared steps; one loop with a hash lookup inside is O of n. Remember: Ask yourself: how many times does the innermost line run as n doubles?

bites.title: Arrays vs Linked Lists
bites.tldr: Arrays give instant index access; linked lists give cheap inserts once you're at the right node.
points: Array: contiguous memory, O(1) access by index, O(n) insert or delete in the middle.
Dynamic arrays (ArrayList, Python list) double their capacity, so append is O(1) amortised.
Linked list: O(1) insert or delete given the node, but O(n) to find a position.
Arrays are cache-friendly; linked lists jump around memory.
bites.example: Implementing an LRU cache uses a linked list for O(1) move-to-front plus a hash map to find nodes.
bites.tip: Need random access, use an array. Need lots of splicing at known spots, use a linked list.

quiz.q: Appending to a dynamic array is O(1)…
quiz.why: Occasional resizes cost O(n), but spread over many appends the average is constant.

Need lots of splicing at known spots, use a linked list.

bites.title: Hash Tables
bites.tldr: A hash table maps keys to buckets with a hash function for average O(1) insert, lookup and delete.
points: The hash function turns a key into a bucket index.
Collisions are handled by chaining (lists per bucket) or open addressing (probing).
The load factor (items ÷ buckets) triggers a resize to keep operations fast.
Worst case is O(n) when everything collides; good hashing makes that rare.
bites.example: Two-sum in one pass: store each number's index in a map and look up target − x.
bites.tip: Keys must be immutable and have consistent equals and hashCode.

quiz.q: What happens when a hash table's load factor gets too high?
quiz.why: Growing the bucket array keeps chains short and lookups fast.

Worst case is O of n when everything collides; good hashing makes that rare. Example: Two-sum in one pass: store each number's index in a map and look up target minus x. bites.title: Stacks, Queues and Deques
bites.tldr: A stack is last-in-first-out, a queue is first-in-first-out, and a deque allows both ends.
points: Stack: push and pop at the top. Used for undo, call stacks, matching brackets and DFS.
Queue: enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front. Used for BFS, task scheduling and buffering.
Deque: push and pop at both ends in O(1), the basis of sliding-window maximums.
In Java use ArrayDeque; in Python use collections.deque.
bites.example: Checking ( [ ] ) uses a stack: push openers, pop and compare on closers.
bites.tip: Recursion is an implicit stack; BFS needs an explicit queue.

quiz.q: Which structure does breadth-first search use?
quiz.why: BFS processes nodes in discovery order: first in, first out.

Example: Checking uses a stack: push openers, pop and compare on closers. Remember: Recursion is an implicit stack; BFS needs an explicit queue.

bites.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
bites.tldr: A binary heap keeps the smallest (or largest) item on top with O(log n) insert and remove.
points: Stored as an array: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
Push adds at the end and sifts up; pop moves the last item to the top and sifts down.
Building a heap from n items takes O(n).
Use it for top-k, scheduling, Dijkstra and merging sorted lists.
bites.example: Keep a min-heap of size k to find the k largest items in O(n log k).
bites.tip: Python's heapq is a min-heap; negate values for a max-heap.

quiz.q: Peeking at the minimum of a min-heap costs…
quiz.why: The minimum always sits at the root.

bites.say: Heaps and Priority Queues. A binary heap keeps the smallest (or largest) item on top with O of log n insert and remove. bites.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
bites.tldr: A BST keeps smaller keys on the left and larger on the right, so search follows one path.
points: Traversals: pre-order (node first), in-order (sorted for a BST), post-order (children first), level-order (BFS).
Balanced BSTs (red-black, AVL) guarantee O(log n) operations; unbalanced ones can degrade to O(n).
Height h bounds recursion depth and many costs.
Java's TreeMap and C++'s std::map are balanced BSTs.
bites.example: An in-order walk of a BST prints its keys in sorted order.
bites.tip: Tree problems usually reduce to: what should each node return to its parent?

quiz.q: Which traversal lists BST keys in sorted order?
quiz.why: Left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree gives ascending order.

bites.title: Graph Representations
bites.tldr: Graphs model relationships: nodes (vertices) connected by edges, stored as lists or matrices.
points: Adjacency list: O(V + E) space, best for sparse graphs (most real graphs).
Adjacency matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge checks, good for dense graphs.
Edges can be directed or undirected, and weighted or unweighted.
Trees are connected acyclic graphs; DAGs are directed acyclic graphs.
bites.example: A social network with a billion users and a few hundred friends each needs adjacency lists.
bites.tip: Ask early: directed? weighted? can it have cycles? is it connected?

quiz.q: Space for an adjacency matrix with V vertices?
quiz.why: A V by V grid of cells regardless of how many edges exist.

units.title: Algorithms
units.blurb: The recurring ideas behind almost every interview problem.

bites.title: Sorting Algorithms
bites.tldr: Comparison sorts can't beat O(n log n); merge sort, quicksort and heapsort reach it.
points: Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, needs O(n) extra memory.
Quicksort: O(n log n) on average, O(n²) worst case, in place and very fast in practice.
Heapsort: O(n log n) in place, not stable.
Counting and radix sort beat n log n for small integer keys.
bites.formula: Comparison sort lower bound: log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n
bites.example: Java sorts objects with TimSort (a stable merge sort hybrid) and primitives with dual-pivot quicksort.
bites.tip: Stable means equal keys keep their original order, which matters when sorting by several fields.

quiz.q: Which sort is stable and guaranteed O(n log n)?
quiz.why: Merge sort's merge step keeps equal items in order and never degrades.

bites.say: Sorting Algorithms. Comparison sorts can't beat O of n log n; merge sort, quicksort and heapsort reach it. Merge sort: O of n log n always, stable, needs O of n extra memory. Quicksort: O of n log n on average, O of n squared worst case, in place and very fast in practice. Heapsort: O of n log n in place, not stable. Counting and radix sort beat n log n for small integer keys. Any comparison sort needs about n log n comparisons, because there are n factorial possible orders. Example: Java sorts objects with Tim Sort (a stable merge sort hybrid) and primitives with dual-pivot quicksort. Remember: Stable means equal keys keep their original order, which matters when sorting by several fields.

bites.title: Binary Search Beyond Arrays
bites.tldr: Binary search works on any yes/no question that flips exactly once across a sorted range.
points: Classic: find a value in a sorted array in O(log n).
Lower bound: the first index where value ≥ target.
Search on the answer: the smallest capacity, speed or time that makes a check pass.
Careful with mid = (lo + hi) / 2 overflow in Java; use lo + (hi − lo) / 2 or >>>.
bites.example: Smallest truck capacity that ships everything in D days: binary search capacities, check greedily.
bites.tip: Decide whether your range is [lo, hi] or [lo, hi) and stick to it.

quiz.q: Binary search on the answer requires the check to be…
quiz.why: If x works then every bigger x works, so the answers split into fail and then pass.

bites.say: Binary Search Beyond Arrays. Binary search works on any yes/no question that flips exactly once across a sorted range. Classic: find a value in a sorted array in O of log n. Lower bound: the first index where value greater than or equal to target. Search on the answer: the smallest capacity, speed or time that makes a check pass. Careful with mid equals (lo plus hi) over 2 overflow in Java; use lo plus (hi minus lo) over 2 or shifted right by >. Example: Smallest truck capacity that ships everything in D days: binary search capacities, check greedily. Remember: Decide whether your range is lo, hi or lo, hi) and stick to it.

bites.title: Recursion and Divide and Conquer
bites.tldr: Solve a problem by solving smaller copies of it, then combining the answers.
points: Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it.
Divide and conquer: split, solve the parts, combine (merge sort, quicksort, binary search).
Master theorem: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) gives the running time of many recurrences.
Deep recursion can overflow the stack; convert to iteration if needed.
bites.formula: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) ⇒ T(n) = O(n log n)
bites.example: Merge sort splits in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges in linear time.
bites.tip: Trust the recursion: assume the smaller call works and focus on combining.

quiz.q: What prevents infinite recursion?
quiz.why: The base case answers directly without recursing.

bites.say: Recursion and Divide and Conquer. Solve a problem by solving smaller copies of it, then combining the answers. Every recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. Divide and conquer: split, solve the parts, combine (merge sort, quicksort, binary search). Master theorem: T of n equals aT(n/b) plus f of n gives the running time of many recurrences. Deep recursion can overflow the stack; convert to iteration if needed. Two half-size subproblems plus linear combining work gives n log n. Example: Merge sort splits in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges in linear time. Remember: Trust the recursion: assume the smaller call works and focus on combining.

bites.title: Dynamic Programming
bites.tldr: DP solves overlapping subproblems once and reuses their answers.
points: Two ingredients: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
Top-down: recursion plus memoization. Bottom-up: fill a table in dependency order.
Define the state precisely, write the transition, set the base cases, then pick the answer cell.
Often only the last row or last few values are needed, giving O(1) or O(n) space.
bites.example: Climbing stairs: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), with just two rolling variables.
bites.tip: If brute force recomputes the same calls, cache them and you're doing DP.

quiz.q: Memoization is…
quiz.why: Top-down DP stores each subproblem's answer the first time it's computed.

bites.title: Greedy Algorithms
bites.tldr: Greedy algorithms take the best-looking step now and never revisit it.
points: They work only when a local choice is provably part of some optimal solution.
Classic wins: interval scheduling by earliest end, Huffman coding, Dijkstra, Kruskal.
Prove it with an exchange argument: swapping in the greedy choice never makes things worse.
When greedy fails, such as coin systems like {1, 3, 4} for amount 6, use DP.
bites.example: To keep the most non-overlapping meetings, always pick the one that ends first.
bites.tip: Try to break your greedy idea with a small counterexample before coding it.

quiz.q: Greedy fails for making 6 with coins {1, 3, 4} because it picks…
quiz.why: Greedy takes 4 first and needs three coins; the optimum 3 + 3 uses two.

bites.title: BFS vs DFS
bites.tldr: BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS dives deep first.
points: BFS uses a queue and visits nodes in order of distance.
DFS uses recursion or a stack: good for connectivity, cycles, topological order and backtracking.
Both run in O(V + E) with a visited set.
On grids, neighbours are the 4 (or 8) adjacent cells.
bites.example: Fewest moves for a knight on a chessboard: BFS. Count islands: DFS or BFS.
bites.tip: Mark a node visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it, to avoid duplicates.

quiz.q: Shortest path in an unweighted graph?
quiz.why: BFS reaches every node first by a path with the fewest edges.

bites.title: Shortest Paths
bites.tldr: Dijkstra handles non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford handles negatives; Floyd-Warshall handles all pairs.
points: Dijkstra: a min-heap of (distance, node), O(E log V).
Bellman-Ford: relax every edge V − 1 times, O(V·E), and detects negative cycles.
Floyd-Warshall: dynamic programming over intermediate nodes, O(V³).
A* adds a heuristic to Dijkstra to aim at the goal faster.
bites.example: Routing packets or maps with travel times: Dijkstra or A*.
bites.tip: A negative edge breaks Dijkstra's assumption that a settled node is final.

quiz.q: Which algorithm detects negative cycles?
quiz.why: If a V-th round of relaxation still improves a distance, a negative cycle exists.

bites.title: Topological Sort
bites.tldr: A topological order lists a DAG's nodes so every edge points forward.
points: Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take nodes with in-degree 0.
DFS version: record nodes after visiting their children, then reverse the list.
If not every node gets output, the graph has a cycle.
Used for build systems, course prerequisites and task scheduling.
bites.example: Compile modules so each dependency is built before the modules that need it.
bites.tip: A topological order exists if and only if the directed graph has no cycle.

quiz.q: Kahn's algorithm starts with nodes that have…
quiz.why: Nodes with no prerequisites can safely go first.

units.title: Systems
units.blurb: What really happens underneath your code.

bites.title: Processes vs Threads
bites.tldr: Processes have separate memory; threads share their process's memory and are cheaper to create.
points: A process owns an address space, file handles and at least one thread.
Threads share the heap, so they communicate easily but need synchronisation.
Context switches between threads are cheaper than between processes.
Java 21 virtual threads are cheap enough to create one per request.
bites.example: A browser runs each tab in its own process so one crash doesn't take down the others.
bites.tip: Isolation favours processes; cheap sharing favours threads.

quiz.q: What do threads of the same process share?
quiz.why: Each thread has its own stack and registers, but they share the heap.

bites.title: Race Conditions and Deadlocks
bites.tldr: Races happen when timing changes results; deadlocks happen when threads wait on each other forever.
points: Race: two threads do read-modify-write on shared data without coordination.
Fix races with locks, atomics, immutability or confinement to one thread.
Deadlock needs four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Prevent deadlocks by always acquiring locks in a global order, or by using timeouts.
bites.example: count++ is three steps (read, add, write); two threads can both read 5 and both write 6.
bites.tip: Lock ordering is the simplest deadlock cure.

quiz.q: Which change breaks the circular-wait condition?
quiz.why: If everyone locks A before B, no cycle of waiting can form.

bites.title: Stack, Heap and Garbage Collection
bites.tldr: The stack holds call frames; the heap holds objects that outlive a single call.
points: Stack allocation is fast and freed automatically when a function returns.
Heap objects are freed manually (C) or by a garbage collector (Java, Python, Go).
Generational GC exploits the fact that most objects die young.
Memory leaks in GC languages come from references you forgot to drop, such as caches and listeners.
bites.example: A static HashMap that only grows keeps every entry reachable, so it's never collected.
bites.tip: Unbounded caches are leaks with good intentions: give them a size or time limit.

quiz.q: A garbage collector frees objects that are…
quiz.why: Anything no longer reachable from roots like stacks and statics can be reclaimed.

bites.title: Virtual Memory and Caching
bites.tldr: Every process sees its own virtual address space; hardware maps pages to physical memory.
points: Pages (often 4 KB) are mapped through page tables, sped up by the TLB.
A page fault loads a page from disk when it isn't in memory.
CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) exploit temporal and spatial locality.
Sequential access through arrays is much faster than pointer chasing.
bites.example: Iterating a 2D array row by row is faster than column by column in row-major languages.
bites.tip: Rough latencies: L1 ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD ~100 µs, a network round trip ~0.5 ms or more.

quiz.q: Spatial locality means…
quiz.why: Caches load whole lines, so neighbouring data comes along for free.

units.title: Networks
units.blurb: How bytes get from one machine to another.

bites.title: TCP vs UDP
bites.tldr: TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP is fast, connectionless and best effort.
points: TCP: three-way handshake, retransmissions, flow and congestion control.
UDP: no handshake, no ordering, no retries; great for real-time media, games and DNS.
QUIC (HTTP/3) builds reliability on top of UDP to avoid head-of-line blocking.
Ports identify the application on a host.
bites.example: A video call prefers a dropped frame over a late one, so it uses UDP or QUIC.
bites.tip: Reliability costs latency; choose based on whether stale data is worse than missing data.

quiz.q: Which protocol guarantees ordered delivery?
quiz.why: TCP numbers its bytes and reorders and retransmits as needed.

bites.title: HTTP and HTTPS
bites.tldr: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol; HTTPS wraps it in TLS for privacy and integrity.
points: Methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
TLS uses certificates to authenticate the server and negotiates session keys.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC.
bites.example: 429 Too Many Requests plus Retry-After tells a client to back off.
bites.tip: GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent; POST usually isn't.

quiz.q: Which status means the client sent invalid input?
quiz.why: 4xx codes blame the request; 400 means Bad Request.

bites.title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
bites.tldr: DNS turns names like example.com into IP addresses through a hierarchy of servers.
points: Resolvers ask root servers, then top-level-domain servers, then authoritative servers.
Answers are cached for their TTL (time to live).
Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verification).

bites.title: SQL vs NoSQL
bites.tldr: Relational databases offer schemas, joins and transactions; NoSQL trades some of that for scale or flexibility.
points: SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL): tables, foreign keys, joins, strong consistency.
Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): blazing fast lookups by key.
Document (MongoDB): flexible JSON-like records.
Wide-column (Cassandra) and graph (Neo4j) stores serve specialised access patterns.
bites.example: Orders and payments belong in PostgreSQL; session tokens and rate-limit counters fit Redis.
bites.tip: Start relational unless the access pattern clearly demands otherwise.

quiz.q: Which store is best for very fast lookups by a single key?
quiz.why: Key-value stores are optimised for get and put by key.

bites.title: Indexes
bites.tldr: An index is a sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that turns full table scans into fast lookups.
points: B-tree indexes support equality, range queries and ORDER BY.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: (a, b) helps queries on a, or on a and b, not on b alone.
Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and use space.
Use EXPLAIN to see whether a query uses an index.
bites.example: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC is served perfectly by an index on (user_id, created_at).
bites.tip: Index the columns you filter and join on, not every column.

quiz.q: A composite index on (a, b) helps a query filtering only on…

bites.title: Transactions, ACID and Isolation

points: ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.
Anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, lost updates.
Levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable.

bites.example: Two clerks editing the same order: a version column makes the second save fail instead of overwriting.
bites.tip: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed; know your database's default.

quiz.q: Which isolation level prevents all anomalies?
quiz.why: Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

bites.title: P, NP and NP-Complete
bites.tldr: P problems are solvable quickly; NP solutions are checkable quickly; NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP.
points: P: polynomial-time solvable, like sorting or shortest paths.
NP: a proposed answer can be verified in polynomial time.
NP-complete examples: SAT, travelling salesman (decision version), graph coloring, knapsack.
If any NP-complete problem had a fast algorithm, they all would: P would equal NP.
bites.example: Sudoku is easy to check but hard to solve in general: it's NP-complete for n² × n² boards.
bites.tip: In interviews, recognising an NP-hard problem justifies heuristics or exponential search on small inputs.

quiz.q: NP means a solution can be…
quiz.why: NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial: verification is the easy part.

bites.title: How Code Becomes a Program
bites.tldr: Compilers translate source code through lexing, parsing, analysis, optimisation and code generation.
points: Lexer: characters to tokens. Parser: tokens to a syntax tree.
Semantic analysis checks types and scopes.
Optimisers inline functions, remove dead code and unroll loops.
The JVM interprets bytecode, then JIT-compiles hot methods to machine code.
bites.example: Java compiles to bytecode once; the JVM's JIT compiles hot loops to native code at run time.
bites.tip: Interpreters run code directly; compilers translate it ahead of time; JITs do both.

quiz.q: Which stage builds the syntax tree?
quiz.why: The parser checks grammar and produces the tree.

bites.title: OOP and SOLID
bites.tldr: Object-oriented design bundles data with behaviour; SOLID principles keep designs flexible.
points: Encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction are the four pillars.
S: single responsibility. O: open for extension, closed for modification. L: Liskov substitution.
I: interface segregation (small, focused interfaces). D: depend on abstractions, not concretions.
Favour composition over inheritance.
bites.example: Injecting a PaymentGateway interface lets you swap Stripe for a fake in tests.
bites.tip: If a class is hard to name, it probably has more than one responsibility.

quiz.q: 'Depend on abstractions, not concretions' is which principle?
quiz.why: Dependency inversion makes high-level code independent of low-level details.

bites.title: Hashing vs Encryption
bites.tldr: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible with a key.
points: Store passwords with slow, salted hashes: bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2, never SHA-256 alone.
Symmetric encryption (AES) uses one shared key; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses a public/private key pair.
Digital signatures prove who sent a message and that it wasn't changed.
TLS uses asymmetric crypto to agree on a symmetric session key.
bites.example: A leaked bcrypt table forces attackers to brute-force each salted password slowly.
bites.tip: Never roll your own crypto; use vetted libraries.

quiz.q: Which is appropriate for storing passwords?
quiz.why: bcrypt is slow and salted on purpose, which defeats rainbow tables and brute force.

bites.title: Top Web Security Risks
bites.tldr: Most breaches come from a few classic mistakes: injection, broken access control and leaked secrets.
points: SQL injection: always use parameterised queries.
XSS: escape output and use a Content-Security-Policy.
CSRF: SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens for cookie-authenticated forms.
Broken access control: check authorisation on the server for every object, not just in the UI.
bites.example: /api/invoices/124 must verify the invoice belongs to the caller, or users can read each other's invoices.
bites.tip: Validate input, encode output, and enforce authorisation on the server.

quiz.q: The main defence against SQL injection is…
quiz.why: Parameters keep user input as data, never as executable SQL.

units.title: Foundations of Machine Learning
units.blurb: The vocabulary every ML conversation starts with.

bites.title: What Is Machine Learning?
bites.tldr: Machine learning fits a function to data instead of writing the rules by hand.
points: Supervised learning: learn from labelled examples (spam or not, house prices).
Unsupervised learning: find structure without labels (clusters, embeddings).
Reinforcement learning: learn actions from rewards by trial and error.
Self-supervised learning creates labels from the data itself, such as predicting the next word.
bites.example: An email filter learns from thousands of emails users marked as spam.
bites.tip: Every ML system is data plus a model plus a loss plus an optimiser.

quiz.q: Predicting the next word in text with no human labels is…
quiz.why: The training text supplies its own labels: each next word.

Remember: Every ML system is data plus a model plus a loss plus an optimiser.

bites.title: Train, Validation and Test Sets
bites.tldr: Split data so you can measure how well a model generalises to data it has never seen.
points: Training set: fit the parameters.
Validation set: tune hyperparameters and choose models.
Test set: one final, honest estimate. Touch it once.
Cross-validation rotates the validation fold when data is scarce.
bites.example: A typical split is 80 / 10 / 10; for time series, split by time so you never train on the future.
bites.tip: Data leakage, where test information sneaks into training, is the silent killer of ML projects.

quiz.q: Which set should you use to choose hyperparameters?
quiz.why: Tuning on the test set makes its score optimistic.

Example: A typical split is 80 over 10 over 10; for time series, split by time so you never train on the future. bites.title: Bias, Variance and Overfitting
bites.tldr: Underfitting is high bias, overfitting is high variance; the goal is the sweet spot between them.
points: High bias: the model is too simple, so error is high on both training and test data.
High variance: the model memorises the training data, so training error is low but test error is high.
Fix overfitting with more data, regularisation, dropout, early stopping or simpler models.
Fix underfitting with richer features or bigger models.
bites.example: A degree-15 polynomial through 10 points fits perfectly and predicts terribly.
bites.tip: Plot training and validation curves: a widening gap means overfitting.

quiz.q: Training accuracy 99%, test accuracy 60% suggests…
quiz.why: A big gap between training and test performance means high variance.

Fix overfitting with more data, regularisation, dropout, early stopping or simpler models. Fix underfitting with richer features or bigger models. Expected error equals bias squared, plus variance, plus irreducible noise. Example: A degree minus 15 polynomial through 10 points fits perfectly and predicts terribly. Remember: Plot training and validation curves: a widening gap means overfitting.

bites.title: Loss Functions and Gradient Descent
bites.tldr: Training minimises a loss by repeatedly stepping parameters against the gradient.
points: Mean squared error for regression; cross-entropy for classification.
Gradient descent: θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), where η is the learning rate.
Mini-batch SGD uses a small batch per step: noisy but fast.
Adam adapts per-parameter step sizes and is the default for deep learning.
bites.example: Too high a learning rate makes the loss bounce or explode; too low makes training crawl.
bites.tip: If the loss is NaN, lower the learning rate and check for division by zero or log of zero.

quiz.q: The learning rate controls…
quiz.why: It scales how far each update moves the parameters.

bites.say: Loss Functions and Gradient Descent. Training minimises a loss by repeatedly stepping parameters against the gradient. Mean squared error for regression; cross-entropy for classification. bites.title: Regularization
bites.tldr: Regularization adds a penalty that discourages overly complex models.
points: L2 (ridge, weight decay) shrinks weights smoothly.
L1 (lasso) pushes some weights exactly to zero, selecting features.
Dropout randomly zeroes activations during training.
Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving.
bites.example: With 10,000 features and 500 rows, L1 keeps just the handful of features that matter.
bites.tip: λ is a hyperparameter: tune it on the validation set.

quiz.q: Which penalty tends to make weights exactly zero?
quiz.why: L1's sharp corner at zero makes sparse solutions likely.

Total loss equals data loss plus lambda times the squared size of the weights. Example: With 10, 000 features and 500 rows, L1 keeps just the handful of features that matter. units.title: Classic Models & Metrics
units.blurb: Strong baselines and how to measure them honestly.

bites.title: Linear and Logistic Regression
bites.tldr: Linear regression predicts numbers; logistic regression predicts probabilities for classes.
points: Linear: ŷ = w·x + b, trained with squared error.
Logistic: p = σ(w·x + b), where the sigmoid squashes values into (0, 1).
Trained with cross-entropy (log loss).
Coefficients are interpretable: the effect of one feature, holding the others fixed.
bites.example: Predicting churn probability from usage features is logistic regression's home turf.
bites.tip: Always try a simple linear baseline before a deep network.

quiz.q: Logistic regression outputs…
quiz.why: The sigmoid maps scores into the 0 to 1 range.

Coefficients are interpretable: the effect of one feature, holding the others fixed. The sigmoid of z equals one over one plus e to the minus z. Example: Predicting churn probability from usage features is logistic regression's home turf. Remember: Always try a simple linear baseline before a deep network.

bites.title: Decision Trees and Ensembles
bites.tldr: Trees split data with if-then questions; ensembles of trees are top performers on tabular data.
points: A tree picks the split that most reduces impurity (Gini or entropy).
Random forest: many deep trees on bootstrapped data with random features, then vote. This reduces variance.
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM): shallow trees added one by one to fix the previous errors. This reduces bias.
Trees need little preprocessing: no feature scaling required.
bites.example: Credit scoring and fraud models often use gradient-boosted trees.
bites.tip: For tables of numbers and categories, try gradient boosting before deep learning.

quiz.q: Bagging (random forests) mainly reduces…
quiz.why: Averaging many noisy trees cancels out their individual variance.

bites.title: k-NN and k-Means
bites.tldr: k-NN classifies by the nearest labelled neighbours; k-means groups unlabelled points into k clusters.
points: k-NN: no training, slow predictions, sensitive to feature scaling.
k-means: alternate between assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to its points' mean.
k-means needs k chosen up front (elbow method, silhouette score).
Both rely on a distance metric: Euclidean, cosine and so on.
bites.example: Segment customers into 5 groups by spending habits with k-means.
bites.tip: Standardise features first, or the feature with the largest units dominates the distance.

quiz.q: Which one is unsupervised?
quiz.why: k-means clusters without needing labels.

bites.title: Precision, Recall and F1
bites.tldr: Accuracy hides problems on imbalanced data; precision and recall reveal them.
points: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the items you flagged, how many were right?
Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the true items, how many did you catch?
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds.
bites.example: A cancer screen favours recall (miss nothing); a spam filter favours precision (don't hide real mail).
bites.tip: Choose the metric from the cost of each mistake, not from habit.

quiz.q: A model that flags nothing on 1%-positive data has 99% accuracy and recall of…
quiz.why: It catches none of the positives.

units.blurb: The architectures behind modern AI.

bites.title: Neural Networks
bites.tldr: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums and non-linear activations.
points: Each neuron computes an activation of w·x + b.
Non-linear activations (ReLU, GELU) let networks model curved relationships.
Depth builds hierarchical features: edges, then shapes, then objects.
The universal approximation theorem: enough units can approximate any continuous function.
bites.formula: h = ReLU(Wx + b), ReLU(z) = max(0, z)
bites.example: Without activations, stacking 10 linear layers is still just one linear layer.
bites.tip: Activations are what make deep learning more than linear algebra.

quiz.q: Why do networks need non-linear activations?
opts: Otherwise layers collapse into one linear map
quiz.why: A composition of linear maps is linear.

bites.title: Backpropagation
bites.tldr: Backpropagation computes every weight's gradient efficiently using the chain rule, from the output back.
points: Forward pass: compute the outputs and the loss.
Backward pass: propagate ∂L/∂(activation) layer by layer with the chain rule.
Autograd frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) do this automatically.
Vanishing or exploding gradients are tamed with ReLU, normalisation, residual connections and careful initialisation.
bites.example: Residual connections in ResNets and transformers give gradients a shortcut back through the network.
bites.tip: Backprop is the chain rule plus caching intermediate values.

quiz.q: Backpropagation is an application of…
quiz.why: Gradients of composed functions multiply along the chain.

The derivative of the loss with respect to a weight equals the derivative of the loss with respect to the output, times the derivative of the output with respect to the weight. bites.title: Convolutional Networks
bites.tldr: CNNs slide small learned filters over images, sharing weights across positions.
points: Convolutions detect local patterns anywhere in the image (translation equivariance).
Pooling or strides shrink spatial size while channels grow.
Far fewer parameters than fully connected layers on pixels.
Vision transformers now rival CNNs on large datasets.
bites.example: A 3×3 edge-detector filter applied across the whole image is one convolution channel.
bites.tip: Convolution is a sliding window with learned weights.

quiz.q: Weight sharing in CNNs means…
opts: each pixel has its own weights
the same filter is reused at every position
quiz.why: One filter scans the whole image, so it detects a pattern anywhere.

bites.title: Recurrent Networks and Their Limits
bites.tldr: RNNs process sequences step by step with a hidden state, but struggle with long-range dependencies.
points: The hidden state carries memory: h_t = f(h_(t−1), x_t).
LSTM and GRU gates help preserve information over longer spans.
Sequential processing can't be parallelised across time steps.
Transformers replaced RNNs for most language tasks.
bites.example: Translating long sentences with plain RNNs lost details from the beginning of the sentence.
bites.tip: Remember RNNs as the reason attention was invented.

quiz.q: A key weakness of RNNs is…
quiz.why: Each step depends on the previous hidden state.

The hidden state carries memory: h t equals f(h_(t minus 1), x t). LSTM and GRU gates help preserve information over longer spans. Sequential processing can't be parallelised across time steps. Transformers replaced RNNs for most language tasks. Example: Translating long sentences with plain RNNs lost details from the beginning of the sentence. Remember: Remember RNNs as the reason attention was invented.

bites.title: Attention and Transformers
bites.tldr: Attention lets every token look at every other token and weigh how relevant each one is.
points: Each token makes a query, a key and a value vector.
Scores are query · key, scaled by √d and softmaxed; the output is the weighted sum of values.
Multi-head attention runs several attention patterns in parallel.
Transformers stack attention plus feed-forward layers with residuals and normalisation; they parallelise well on GPUs.
bites.example: In 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big', attention helps link 'it' to 'trophy'.
bites.tip: Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which is why long context is expensive.

quiz.q: Why divide by √d in attention?
opts: To keep dot products from growing too large for the softmax
quiz.why: Large dot products saturate the softmax and shrink gradients.

bites.say: Attention and Transformers. Attention lets every token look at every other token and weigh how relevant each one is. Each token makes a query, a key and a value vector. Scores are query times key, scaled by the square root of d and softmaxed; the output is the weighted sum of values. Multi-head attention runs several attention patterns in parallel. Transformers stack attention plus feed-forward layers with residuals and normalisation; they parallelise well on GPUs. Attention of Q, K and V equals the softmax of Q times K transposed, divided by the square root of d, times V. Example: In 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big', attention helps link 'it' to 'trophy'. Remember: Attention cost grows with the square of sequence length, which is why long context is expensive.

bites.title: Embeddings
bites.tldr: Embeddings map words, sentences, images or users to vectors where similar things sit close together.
points: Learned by models: word2vec, sentence transformers, CLIP for images and text.
Similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot products.
They power semantic search, recommendations, clustering and RAG.
The dimension is often 384 to 3072.
bites.example: 'car' and 'automobile' end up near each other even though they share no letters.
bites.tip: Only compare embeddings that came from the same model.

quiz.q: Cosine similarity of 1 means two vectors…
quiz.why: The angle between them is zero.

bites.title: How LLMs Are Trained
bites.tldr: Large language models are pretrained to predict the next token, then tuned to follow instructions.
points: Pretraining: next-token prediction on trillions of tokens.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): learn from curated prompt and response examples.
Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO) aligns outputs with human preferences.
Scaling laws: loss falls predictably as you scale parameters, data and compute together.
bites.example: A pretrained model continues text; an instruction-tuned model answers the question.
bites.tip: Most capability comes from pretraining; tuning shapes behaviour.

quiz.q: RLHF primarily aims to…
quiz.why: It optimises the model toward responses people rate higher.

bites.title: Tokens, Temperature and Decoding
bites.tldr: LLMs read and write tokens (sub-word pieces) and pick each next token from a probability distribution.
points: A token is roughly ¾ of an English word; costs and limits are counted in tokens.
Temperature rescales logits: low is focused and repeatable, high is diverse and creative.
Top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling cut off unlikely tokens.
Greedy decoding picks the most likely token every time.
bites.example: Use temperature 0 for extraction or classification; around 0.7 or more for brainstorming.
bites.tip: Lower temperature lowers variance, but not hallucinations caused by missing knowledge.

quiz.q: Raising the temperature makes outputs…
quiz.why: It flattens the distribution, so less likely tokens get picked more often.

bites.title: Reinforcement Learning
bites.tldr: An agent learns a policy that maximises long-term reward by interacting with an environment.
points: Core loop: state → action → reward and next state.
Value-based methods (Q-learning) estimate how good each action is.
Policy-gradient methods (PPO) adjust the policy directly.
The exploration versus exploitation trade-off: try new things or use what works.
bites.formula: Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α [r + γ max Q(s′, a′) − Q(s, a)]
bites.example: Game-playing agents and RLHF for language models both use reinforcement learning.
bites.tip: γ, the discount factor, decides how much the agent values future rewards.

quiz.q: Exploration means…
quiz.why: Without exploration, an agent can get stuck on a mediocre strategy.

bites.title: Classic AI: Search and Reasoning
bites.tldr: Before machine learning, AI meant search, logic and planning, and these ideas still matter.
points: Uninformed search: BFS, DFS, uniform-cost search.
Informed search: A* uses g(n) + h(n) with an admissible heuristic.
Adversarial search: minimax with alpha-beta pruning for games.
Constraint satisfaction: backtracking with constraint propagation (sudoku, scheduling).
bites.example: GPS navigation uses A*-like search with straight-line distance as the heuristic.
bites.tip: An admissible heuristic never overestimates, which keeps A* optimal.

quiz.q: Alpha-beta pruning speeds up…
quiz.why: It skips branches that can't change the minimax result.

bites.title: Responsible AI
bites.tldr: Real-world AI must be fair, private, safe and accountable, not just accurate.
points: Bias in data becomes bias in predictions: evaluate per group.

Explainability tools (SHAP, feature importance) help debug and justify decisions.
Keep humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions.
bites.example: A hiring model trained on past hires can learn to replicate past discrimination.
bites.tip: Measure fairness metrics as seriously as accuracy.

quiz.q: A model performs well overall but poorly for one demographic group. The first step is to…
opts: evaluate metrics per group and investigate the data
quiz.why: Slice-based evaluation reveals hidden failures.

units.title: Linear Algebra
units.blurb: The language of data, graphics and machine learning.

bites.title: Vectors and Dot Products
bites.tldr: A vector is a list of numbers with a direction and length; the dot product measures alignment.
points: Length: ‖v‖ = √(v₁² + … + vₙ²).
Dot product: a · b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = ‖a‖‖b‖ cos θ.
A dot product of zero means the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal).
A projection of a onto b keeps only the part of a pointing along b.
bites.tip: Cosine similarity is just the dot product of unit vectors.

quiz.q: If a · b = 0 (both non-zero), the vectors are…

bites.say: Vectors and Dot Products. A vector is a list of numbers with a direction and length; the dot product measures alignment. Length: norm v norm equals the square root of (v sub 1 squared +... + v sub n squared ). Dot product: a times b equals sigma a sub i b sub i equals norm a norm norm b norm cos theta. A dot product of zero means the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal). A projection of a onto b keeps only the part of a pointing along b. a dot b equals the length of a times the length of b times the cosine of the angle between them. Example: (1, 2) times (3, 4) equals 3 plus 8 equals 11. Remember: Cosine similarity is just the dot product of unit vectors.

bites.title: Matrices as Transformations
bites.tldr: A matrix transforms vectors: rotating, scaling, shearing or projecting them.
points: Matrix times vector: each output entry is a row dotted with the vector.
Matrix multiplication composes transformations; it's not commutative (AB ≠ BA in general).
The identity matrix I leaves vectors unchanged.
(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
bites.example: The 2×2 matrix [[0, −1], [1, 0]] rotates the plane by 90° counterclockwise.
bites.tip: Shapes must chain: (m×n)(n×p) gives an m×p result.

quiz.q: A 3×2 matrix times a 2×4 matrix has shape…
quiz.why: The inner dimensions match (2), and the outer ones remain.

bites.say: Matrices as Transformations. A matrix transforms vectors: rotating, scaling, shearing or projecting them. Matrix times vector: each output entry is a row dotted with the vector. Matrix multiplication composes transformations; it's not commutative (AB not equal to BA in general). The identity matrix I leaves vectors unchanged. (AB)ᵀ equals BᵀAᵀ and (AB) inverse equals B inverse A inverse. Entry i, j of A times B is the sum over k of A i k times B k j. Example: The 2 times 2 matrix 0, minus 1, 1, 0 rotates the plane by 90 degrees counterclockwise. Remember: Shapes must chain: (m times n)(n times p) gives an m times p result.

bites.title: Determinants and Inverses
bites.tldr: The determinant measures how a matrix scales area or volume; zero means it squashes space flat.
points: For 2×2: det [[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc.
det = 0 means the matrix is not invertible (singular).
det(AB) = det(A)·det(B).
Solving Ax = b uses elimination in practice, not computing A⁻¹.
bites.example: det [[2, 1], [4, 2]] = 4 − 4 = 0, so the columns are parallel and there's no inverse.
bites.tip: A negative determinant means the transformation also flips orientation.

quiz.q: A matrix with determinant 0 is…
quiz.why: It collapses some dimension, so it can't be undone.

bites.say: Determinants and Inverses. The determinant measures how a matrix scales area or volume; zero means it squashes space flat. For 2 times 2: det a, b, c, d equals ad minus bc. det equals 0 means the matrix is not invertible (singular). det(AB) equals det(A) times det(B). Solving Ax equals b uses elimination in practice, not computing A inverse. The inverse of a two by two matrix is one over a d minus b c, times the matrix d, minus b, minus c, a. Example: det 2, 1, 4, 2 equals 4 minus 4 equals 0, so the columns are parallel and there's no inverse. Remember: A negative determinant means the transformation also flips orientation.

bites.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
bites.tldr: Eigenvectors keep their direction under a transformation; eigenvalues say how much they stretch.
points: Av = λv for a non-zero v.
Find λ from det(A − λI) = 0.
Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
Used in PCA, PageRank, stability analysis and vibration modes.
bites.example: [[2, 0], [0, 3]] stretches the x-axis by 2 and the y-axis by 3: eigenvalues 2 and 3.
bites.tip: PageRank is the dominant eigenvector of the web's link matrix.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues solve…
quiz.why: λ is an eigenvalue exactly when A − λI is singular.

bites.say: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors. Eigenvectors keep their direction under a transformation; eigenvalues say how much they stretch. Av equals lambda v for a non-zero v. Find lambda from det(A minus lambda I) equals 0. Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. Used in PCA, Page Rank, stability analysis and vibration modes. A times v equals lambda times v. Example: 2, 0, 0, 3 stretches the x-axis by 2 and the y-axis by 3: eigenvalues 2 and 3. Remember: Page Rank is the dominant eigenvector of the web's link matrix.

bites.title: SVD and PCA
bites.tldr: SVD factors any matrix into rotate, scale, rotate; PCA uses it to find the main directions of variation.
points: SVD: A = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U and V and non-negative singular values in Σ.
PCA: centre the data, then take the top singular vectors (principal components).
Keeping the top-k components gives the best rank-k approximation.
Applications: compression, denoising, visualisation, recommender systems.
bites.example: Projecting 1000-dimensional embeddings onto 2 principal components lets you plot them.
bites.tip: Always centre (and usually scale) features before PCA.

quiz.q: PCA's first principal component points in the direction of…
quiz.why: It captures the most spread in the data.

SVD: A equals U sigma Vᵀ with orthogonal U and V and non-negative singular values in sigma. PCA: centre the data, then take the top singular vectors (principal components). Keeping the top-k components gives the best rank-k approximation. Applications: compression, denoising, visualisation, recommender systems. A equals U times Sigma times V transposed. units.title: Probability
units.blurb: Reasoning precisely about uncertainty.

bites.title: Probability Rules
bites.tldr: Probabilities add for 'or' (minus overlap) and multiply for 'and' when events are independent.
points: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Independent: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B).
Conditional: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
bites.example: The chance of at least one six in 4 rolls is 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518.
bites.tip: For 'at least one', compute the complement: 1 − P(none).

quiz.q: Two fair coin flips: P(two heads)?
quiz.why: Independent: 1/2 × 1/2.

bites.say: Probability Rules. Probabilities add for 'or' (minus overlap) and multiply for 'and' when events are independent. P of A or B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A and B. Independent: P of A and B equals P of A times P of B. Conditional: P of A | B equals P of A and B divided by P of B. Complement: P of not A equals 1 minus P of A. The probability of A given B equals the probability of A and B, divided by the probability of B. Example: The chance of at least one six in 4 rolls is 1 minus (5 over 6) to the fourth approximately 0.518. Remember: For 'at least one', compute the complement: 1 minus P of none.

bites.title: Bayes' Theorem
bites.tldr: Bayes' rule updates a belief with new evidence: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
points: P(H | E) = P(E | H)·P(H) / P(E).
Base rates matter: a rare condition stays fairly unlikely even after a positive test.
Naive Bayes classifiers assume features are independent given the class.
This is the foundation of Bayesian inference and spam filtering.
bites.formula: P(H | E) = P(E | H) · P(H) / P(E)
bites.example: A 99%-accurate test for a 1-in-1000 disease: a positive result means only about a 9% chance of disease.
bites.tip: Draw 1000 imaginary people and count them; it beats juggling formulas.

quiz.q: In Bayes' rule, P(H) is called the…
quiz.why: It's your belief before seeing the evidence.

bites.say: Bayes' Theorem. Bayes' rule updates a belief with new evidence: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. P of H | E equals P of E | H times P of H divided by P of E. Base rates matter: a rare condition stays fairly unlikely even after a positive test. Naive Bayes classifiers assume features are independent given the class. This is the foundation of Bayesian inference and spam filtering. The probability of the hypothesis given the evidence equals the probability of the evidence given the hypothesis, times the prior, divided by the probability of the evidence. Example: A 99 percent-accurate test for a 1-in minus 1000 disease: a positive result means only about a 9 percent chance of disease. Remember: Draw 1000 imaginary people and count them; it beats juggling formulas.

bites.title: Key Distributions
bites.tldr: A few distributions model most real randomness: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential.
points: Binomial(n, p): successes in n independent trials; mean np.
Poisson(λ): counts of rare events per interval; mean = variance = λ.
Normal(μ, σ²): bell curve; about 68%, 95% and 99.7% within 1, 2 and 3 σ.
Exponential(λ): waiting time between Poisson events; memoryless.
bites.example: Requests per second to a web server are roughly Poisson; times between requests are exponential.
bites.tip: The 68-95-99.7 rule gives quick sanity checks on normal data.

quiz.q: Which distribution is memoryless?
quiz.why: The chance of waiting another minute doesn't depend on how long you've waited.

bites.say: Key Distributions. A few distributions model most real randomness: Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential. Binomial(n, p): successes in n independent trials; mean np. Poisson( lambda ): counts of rare events per interval; mean equals variance equals lambda. Normal( mu, sigma squared ): bell curve; about 68 percent, 95 percent and 99.7 percent within 1, 2 and 3 sigma. Exponential( lambda ): waiting time between Poisson events; memoryless. Example: Requests per second to a web server are roughly Poisson; times between requests are exponential. Remember: The 68-95-99.7 rule gives quick sanity checks on normal data.

bites.title: Expectation and Variance
bites.tldr: Expectation is the long-run average; variance measures spread around it.
points: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, and E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always.
Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
For independent X and Y: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y).
Standard deviation σ = √Var, in the same units as X.
bites.example: A fair die has E = 3.5 and Var = 35/12 ≈ 2.92.
bites.tip: Linearity of expectation holds even for dependent variables, which makes many puzzles easy.

quiz.q: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] requires X and Y to be…
quiz.why: Linearity of expectation needs no independence.

bites.say: Expectation and Variance. Expectation is the long-run average; variance measures spread around it. E at aX plus b equals aE at X plus b, and E at X plus Y equals E at X plus E at Y always. Var(X) equals E at X squared minus (E at X) squared. For independent X and Y: Var(X plus Y) equals Var(X) plus Var(Y). Standard deviation sigma equals the square root of Var, in the same units as X. The variance of X equals the expected value of X squared, minus the square of the expected value of X. Example: A fair die has E equals 3.5 and Var equals 35 over 12 approximately 2.92. Remember: Linearity of expectation holds even for dependent variables, which makes many puzzles easy.

units.title: Statistics
units.blurb: Drawing honest conclusions from data.

bites.title: The Central Limit Theorem
bites.tldr: Averages of many independent samples are approximately normal, whatever the original distribution.
points: The sample mean has mean μ and standard error σ/√n.
This justifies confidence intervals and many tests.
It needs finite variance and enough samples (often n ≥ 30 is fine).
Heavy-tailed data converges slowly.
bites.example: Average page-load time over 1000 users behaves like a normal variable even if single loads are skewed.
bites.tip: Quadrupling the sample size only halves the standard error.

quiz.q: Standard error of the mean scales like…
quiz.why: σ/√n.

bites.say: The Central Limit Theorem. Averages of many independent samples are approximately normal, whatever the original distribution. The sample mean has mean mu and standard error sigma divided by the square root of n. This justifies confidence intervals and many tests. It needs finite variance and enough samples (often n greater than or equal to 30 is fine). Heavy-tailed data converges slowly. The sample mean is approximately normal with mean mu and variance sigma squared over n. Example: Average page-load time over 1000 users behaves like a normal variable even if single loads are skewed. Remember: Quadrupling the sample size only halves the standard error.

bites.title: Hypothesis Tests and p-Values
bites.tldr: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.
points: Set H₀ (no effect) and H₁, choose α (often 0.05), compute the test statistic and p-value.
p < α means reject H₀; it does not prove H₁ or measure the effect size.
Type I error: false positive (probability α). Type II error: false negative (probability β).
A/B tests compare two variants; beware peeking early and running many comparisons.
bites.example: Checking an A/B test daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives a lot.
bites.tip: Always report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p-values.

quiz.q: p = 0.03 means…
opts: Data this extreme happens 3% of the time if H₀ is true
quiz.why: It's a statement about the data under the null hypothesis.

bites.say: Hypothesis Tests and p-Values. A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. Set H sub 0 (no effect) and H sub 1, choose alpha (often 0.05), compute the test statistic and p-value. p is less than alpha means reject H sub 0; it does not prove H sub 1 or measure the effect size. Type I error: false positive (probability alpha ). Type II error: false negative (probability beta ). A/B tests compare two variants; beware peeking early and running many comparisons. Example: Checking an A/B test daily and stopping at the first p is less than 0.05 inflates false positives a lot. Remember: Always report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p-values.

bites.title: Confidence Intervals
bites.tldr: A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true value in 95% of repeated studies.
points: Mean ± 1.96 × standard error for large samples.
Wider intervals mean more uncertainty; more data narrows them.
Intervals that exclude zero correspond to a significant difference.
Bootstrapping estimates intervals by resampling the data.
bites.example: Conversion lift of +2% with a 95% CI of [+0.5%, +3.5%] is a solid win.
bites.tip: Report intervals in dashboards; single numbers hide uncertainty.

quiz.q: To halve a confidence interval's width you need roughly…
quiz.why: Width scales with 1/√n.

bites.say: Confidence Intervals. A 95 percent confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true value in 95 percent of repeated studies. Mean plus or minus 1.96 times standard error for large samples. Wider intervals mean more uncertainty; more data narrows them. Intervals that exclude zero correspond to a significant difference. Bootstrapping estimates intervals by resampling the data. The sample mean plus or minus 1.96 times the sample standard deviation over the square root of n. Example: Conversion lift of plus 2 percent with a 95 percent CI of +0.5 percent, +3.5 percent is a solid win. Remember: Report intervals in dashboards; single numbers hide uncertainty.

bites.title: Correlation vs Causation
bites.tldr: Correlation measures linear association; causation needs experiments or careful causal reasoning.
points: Pearson r ranges from −1 to 1; r² is the share of variance explained by a linear fit.
Confounders can create correlation with no causal link.
Randomised experiments (A/B tests) break confounding.
Simpson's paradox: trends can reverse when data is grouped.
bites.example: Ice-cream sales and drownings correlate because both rise in summer.
bites.tip: Ask what third factor could drive both variables.

quiz.q: The best way to establish causation is…
quiz.why: Random assignment makes the groups comparable.

bites.say: Correlation versus Causation. Correlation measures linear association; causation needs experiments or careful causal reasoning. Pearson r ranges from minus 1 to 1; r squared is the share of variance explained by a linear fit. Confounders can create correlation with no causal link. Randomised experiments (A/B tests) break confounding. Simpson's paradox: trends can reverse when data is grouped. Example: Ice-cream sales and drownings correlate because both rise in summer. Remember: Ask what third factor could drive both variables.

units.title: Discrete Math & Number Theory
units.blurb: Exact reasoning about structures and counts.

bites.title: Logic and Proof Techniques
bites.tldr: Proofs build certainty: direct proof, contradiction, contrapositive and induction.
points: Contrapositive: proving 'not Q ⇒ not P' proves 'P ⇒ Q'.
Contradiction: assume the opposite and derive something impossible.
Induction: prove a base case and that case k implies case k + 1.
Loop invariants are induction applied to code.
bites.example: Induction proves 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.
bites.tip: Use invariants to argue your algorithm is correct in interviews.

quiz.q: The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is…
opts: if not P then not Q
if not Q then not P
quiz.why: It's logically equivalent to the original statement.

bites.say: Logic and Proof Techniques. Proofs build certainty: direct proof, contradiction, contrapositive and induction. Contrapositive: proving 'not Q implies not P' proves 'P implies Q'. Contradiction: assume the opposite and derive something impossible. Induction: prove a base case and that case k implies case k plus 1. Loop invariants are induction applied to code. Example: Induction proves 1 plus 2 +... + n equals n of n plus 1 over 2. Remember: Use invariants to argue your algorithm is correct in interviews.

bites.title: Counting: Permutations and Combinations
bites.tldr: Count arrangements with permutations (order matters) and selections with combinations (order doesn't).
points: n! orderings of n items.
P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)! ordered selections.
C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!) unordered selections.
Pigeonhole principle: n + 1 items in n boxes forces a shared box.
bites.example: Choosing 3 toppings from 10 gives C(10, 3) = 120 pizzas.
bites.tip: The number of subsets of n items is 2ⁿ, the same count as backtracking explores.

quiz.q: How many ways to arrange 4 distinct books on a shelf?

bites.say: Counting: Permutations and Combinations. Count arrangements with permutations (order matters) and selections with combinations (order doesn't). n! orderings of n items. P of n, k equals n! divided by (n minus k)! ordered selections. C of n, k equals n! divided by (k!(n minus k)!) unordered selections. Pigeonhole principle: n plus 1 items in n boxes forces a shared box. n choose k equals n factorial over k factorial times n minus k factorial. Example: Choosing 3 toppings from 10 gives C of 10, 3 equals 120 pizzas. Remember: The number of subsets of n items is 2 to the n, the same count as backtracking explores.

bites.title: Graph Theory Essentials
bites.tldr: Graph theory studies connections: paths, cycles, trees, coloring and flows.
points: Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees = 2 × number of edges.
A tree with n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges.
Euler path: uses every edge once (0 or 2 odd-degree vertices). Hamiltonian path visits every vertex (NP-complete).
Max-flow equals min-cut.
bites.example: A network of 10 routers connected without redundancy (a tree) uses exactly 9 links.
bites.tip: Spot hidden graphs in interview problems: states are nodes, moves are edges.

quiz.q: A tree with 50 nodes has how many edges?
quiz.why: Trees always have n − 1 edges.

bites.say: Graph Theory Essentials. Graph theory studies connections: paths, cycles, trees, coloring and flows. Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2 times number of edges. A tree with n nodes has exactly n minus 1 edges. Euler path: uses every edge once (0 or 2 odd-degree vertices). Hamiltonian path visits every vertex (NP-complete). Max-flow equals min-cut. Example: A network of 10 routers connected without redundancy (a tree) uses exactly 9 links. Remember: Spot hidden graphs in interview problems: states are nodes, moves are edges.

bites.title: Modular Arithmetic
bites.tldr: Modular arithmetic works with remainders, like a clock, and underpins hashing and cryptography.
points: (a + b) mod m and (a · b) mod m can be reduced at every step.
Fast exponentiation computes aᵇ mod m in O(log b).
Fermat's little theorem: a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p) for prime p not dividing a.
RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes.
bites.example: Answers 'modulo 10⁹ + 7' in contests keep huge counts inside 64-bit integers.
bites.tip: In Java, (a % m + m) % m fixes negative remainders.

quiz.q: 17 mod 5 is…

bites.title: GCD, LCM and Primes
bites.tldr: Euclid's algorithm finds the greatest common divisor fast; primes are the building blocks of integers.
points: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), down to gcd(a, 0) = a.
lcm(a, b) = a·b / gcd(a, b).
The Sieve of Eratosthenes lists primes up to n in O(n log log n).
Every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes.
bites.formula: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
bites.tip: To check if n is prime, trial division only needs to go up to √n.

units.title: Beyond: Complex Numbers, Transforms & Optimisation
units.blurb: Powerful tools that show up in AI and systems.

bites.title: Complex Numbers
bites.tldr: Complex numbers a + bi extend the reals with i² = −1 and make rotations simple.
points: Polar form: r(cos θ + i sin θ) = re^(iθ).
Multiplying multiplies lengths and adds angles.
Euler's identity: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0.
Used in signal processing, quantum computing and electrical engineering.
bites.formula: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ
bites.example: Multiplying by i rotates a point 90° counterclockwise in the complex plane.
bites.tip: Think of complex multiplication as rotate-and-scale.

quiz.q: What is i²?
quiz.why: By definition.

bites.title: Fourier Transforms
bites.tldr: The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a sum of sine waves of different frequencies.
points: Time domain ↔ frequency domain.
The FFT computes the discrete transform in O(n log n).
Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency.
Applications: audio, image compression (JPEG uses a cosine transform), fast polynomial multiplication.
bites.example: A spectrum analyser shows which pitches are present in a chord.
bites.tip: When an algorithm convolves big sequences, think FFT.

quiz.q: FFT complexity?
quiz.why: Divide and conquer over even and odd indices.

bites.title: Convex Optimisation
bites.tldr: Convex problems have a single valley, so any local minimum is the global minimum.
points: A function is convex if the line between any two points on its graph lies above the graph.
Gradient descent reliably finds the minimum of convex functions.
Lagrange multipliers handle equality constraints: ∇f = λ∇g.
Neural network losses are non-convex, but SGD still works well in practice.
bites.example: Linear regression's squared-error loss is convex, so it has one best solution.
bites.tip: Convexity is what makes an optimisation problem easy.

quiz.q: For a convex function, a local minimum is…
quiz.why: There's only one valley.

A function is convex if the line between any two points on its graph lies above the graph. Gradient descent reliably finds the minimum of convex functions. Lagrange multipliers handle equality constraints: del f equals lambda del g. Neural network losses are non-convex, but SGD still works well in practice. At the constrained optimum, the gradient of f is lambda times the gradient of the constraint g. Example: Linear regression's squared-error loss is convex, so it has one best solution. bites.title: Information Theory
bites.tldr: Entropy measures uncertainty in bits; cross-entropy measures the cost of using the wrong distribution.
points: Entropy: H(p) = −Σ p log₂ p bits.
Cross-entropy H(p, q) is the classification loss of neural networks.
KL divergence = cross-entropy − entropy ≥ 0, a distance-like gap between distributions.
Compression can't beat entropy on average.
bites.example: A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy; a coin that always lands heads has 0.
bites.tip: Perplexity in language models is 2 to the power of the cross-entropy.

quiz.q: Which loss do most classifiers minimise?
quiz.why: Cross-entropy compares predicted probabilities with the true labels.

Compression can't beat entropy on average. The entropy of p equals minus the sum of p i times log base two of p i. Example: A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy; a coin that always lands heads has 0.
